name: Dudou

lead: A dudou is a single diamond-shaped piece of fabric covering the front of the torso, held by ties at the neck and waist, leaving the back bare. It began as a protective undershirt and became an embroidered women's garment in the Ming and Qing dynasties.

Today it is worn as a halter-style top and in traditional wedding dress, where its embroidered red, pink and green designs and open back shape the outfit. Designers including Versace, Versus and Miu Miu showed variations in 2000.

paras: It is worn like a halter: the neck tie and waist tie are fastened at the back, often over or in place of a top, with embroidery of flowers, butterflies or mandarin ducks as the focus. Wealthier wearers historically used silk or brocade and poorer ones cotton.
No health risks are documented for wearing it as clothing. Historically some women used it to flatten the breasts, and that use was formally banned beginning in Guangdong in 1927.

lead: The dudou (Chinese: 肚兜) is a traditional Chinese garment, a diamond-shaped piece of cloth covering the front of the torso and tied at the neck and waist. It was originally an undershirt with medicinal associations and is today worn as a halter-style top. [1][2]

For appearance, it offers an embroidered, open-backed silhouette in colours such as red, pink and green, often with floral, butterfly or mandarin duck motifs. It remains part of traditional Chinese wedding attire. [2]

Its history runs from earlier Chinese abdominal wraps through the Ming dynasty, when it was popularised from the mid-1300s, to a decline late in the Qing as European corsets and bras replaced it, and a fashion revival from 2000. [2]

paras: A dudou is typically a single diamond-shaped piece of fabric tied at the neck and waist, making it a form of halter top. Wealthier women used silk or brocade, poorer women cotton. Red, pink and green are common, with embroidery of flowers, butterflies or mandarin ducks. [2]
Children wore dudou as well, with girls' versions worn until about age three; pockets often held ginger, musk or herbs, and red was thought to ward off evil spirits. [2]

Wikipedia notes that its development is sometimes credited to Yang Yuhuan, consort of Emperor Xuanzong of the Tang dynasty, when it was called hezi, and that undershirt variants date back to the Qin dynasty. It was popularised under the Ming from the mid-1300s. [2]

Grokipedia, an AI-generated source, similarly describes precursors such as Han-era wraps and Song-era chest wraps, and cautions that the earliest firm evidence of the diamond-shaped form is Ming-era. [1]

During the Ming and Qing it was used to flatten women's breasts; it fell out of favour late in the Qing in favour of European corsets and bras, and that use was formally outlawed beginning in Guangdong in 1927. It inspired the Vietnamese yem and Japanese haragake. [2]

In 2000 variations appeared in the spring collections of Versace, Versus and Miu Miu; Vogue described the Versace pieces as "mischievous handkerchief blouses". Actress Zhang Ziyi later wore dudou as outerwear, a use many older Chinese viewers disapprove of. [2]
